1.0.0.en: Here St. Paul affirms that the apostolic ministry he performs was not entrusted to him by a man, but by God the Father, who accomplished salvation for us through His Son Jesus Christ, our hope that will not disappoint.

1.1.0.en: The Apostle addresses the Epistle to his disciple Timothy, whom he calls “my own son.” The Greek word translated here as “own” is “genesios,” which means genuine or true; so he regards Timothy as a true son to him, and likewise he bears witness to the genuineness of his faith and his labor in preaching the Gospel. As is usual in the epistles of Paul, he asks grace from God for all, and here he adds mercy as well, by which God lifted us out of a state of enmity into sonship. He asks for them the peace that Christ promised to give us, the peace that passes all understanding. And the Apostle here affirms the oneness of the source of grace, mercy and peace, and the oneness of work between the Father and the Son, when he says, “from God our Father and Jesus Christ our Lord.”

1.1.1.en: May you be confident of God who is with you and who commands you to be a light to the world, so that you hold fast to truth and love in all your dealings, even if all the others walk in evil. Do not be shaken, trusting in the power of God that upholds you.

1.2.0.en: After the Apostle was released from his first imprisonment in Rome in AD 63, he went to Macedonia and asked Timothy to remain in Ephesus in order to forbid the strange doctrines preached by some priests and teachers (Acts 20:30) and to bring them back to the right faith, because some preached Judaizing and others preached Gnosticism, as we mentioned in the introduction to the Epistle.

1.3.0.en: Fables: imaginary tales with which the myths of the Greeks and the Romans are filled.

1.3.1.en: Genealogies: the Jews’ pride in tracing the Levites to Aaron or the tribe of Judah to David, and likewise the concern of the Gentiles for their lineage back to great men.

1.3.2.en: Endless: without benefit and without purpose.

1.3.3.en: Questions: the disputes of the Gnostics, who believe that knowledge is salvation, and so argue proudly to establish their opinions. This is utterly far from faith, which is the way of salvation, and from which spiritual studies and inquiries spring.

1.3.4.en: The Apostle warns them to keep away from believing and being influenced by the talk of myths or from boasting in genealogies, because this breeds pride and draws them into harmful disputes that turn them away from building their spiritual life and growing in Christ.

1.4.0.en: Love is the goal of the commandment, and the Lord of glory affirmed this truth in His reply to the lawyer, as it is written in (Mt 22:35-39), that on the commandment of love hang all the Law and the Prophets. And for this love to be genuine, it must spring from a heart sanctified by God’s dwelling in it, from a good intention untouched by any malice, and from sincere faith.

1.5.0.en: If a person turns aside from sincere divine love and from faith, he turns away from the godly life and true witness to talk that profits nothing and to aimless questionings.

1.5.1.en: Examine your love toward others: is it for God’s sake, or according to your personal liking, or does it have material aims? May you care for everyone even if you have no interest in them, be gentle with offenders whom people shun, and pray for all.

1.6.s.en: (3) The Law makes us aware of the need for salvation

1.6.0.en: These people of whom St. Paul speaks are of Jewish origin; they follow position and love of leadership, seek fame and demand honor, while in truth they are far from knowing the goal of the Law. They multiply discussions and disputes, not out of a desire to reach the truth, but in order to impose their authority on people.

1.7.0.en: Uses it lawfully: understands the spirit of the Law and applies it carefully for God’s sake.

1.7.1.en: So that no one misunderstands St. Paul and thinks that he is accusing the Law and condemning it, or condemning teaching as something not good, he affirms that the fault is not in the Law, for it is good and holy, but in its misuse.

1.8.0.en: The Law was made not for the righteous but for the wicked, because the righteous can grasp the commandments of the Law through their natural conscience, whereas for the wicked it is the Law that can keep them from sin by frightening them with punishment. Here the Apostle mentions kinds of wicked people: the lawless, who are sinners ... the disobedient, who are those who break the commandment deliberately ... the ungodly, who are those who commit sin without shame or modesty ... sinners, who are those who commit transgressions ... the unholy, who are those defiled by sins and iniquities ... the profane, who are those who sin without the least reproach from their consciences ... murderers of fathers and mothers, who represent the hardest kinds of hearts ... manslayers, who make light of the lives of others.

1.9.0.en: Whoremongers: those who defile their bodies.

1.9.1.en: Them that defile themselves with mankind: those who are sexually perverse.

1.9.2.en: Menstealers: those who seize the property of others without right. Liars: those who do not tell the truth in pursuit of material gain. Perjured persons: those who do not keep their promise.

1.9.3.en: Whatever is contrary to sound doctrine: those who resist the true teaching. For the sake of these and their like, God gave His Law, that they might feel the need for salvation.

1.10.0.en: Sound doctrine is the joyful good news that shows the greatness of the blessed God, and it is the teaching that St. Paul passed on faithfully, as the divine will willed to make him a faithful witness to the soundness of the teaching.

1.10.1.en: May you benefit from God’s commandments and apply them in your life, for every teaching you hear is a message to you. Do not hurry to rebuke and teach others while forgetting your own personal life.

1.11.0.en: St. Paul thanks God because He counted him faithful and strengthened him and called him to His service despite his unworthiness.

1.12.0.en: In humility St. Paul confesses his former sins before believing, which are:

1.12.1.en: 1- Blaspheming Christ and describing Him as a mere ordinary man.

1.12.2.en: 2- Persecuting the Christians by arresting them, torturing them and killing them.

1.12.3.en: 3- Slandering them with false charges in order to put them on trial and torture them.

1.12.4.en: At the same time God’s great mercy appears in forgiving these sins, and even in turning him into a minister and preacher, because he did these evils from not knowing Christ; and when Christ appeared to him, he repented and turned back from his sins.

1.13.0.en: In addition to making him a minister, God’s grace overflowed upon him with many spiritual gifts and fruits, besides his first enjoying the Christian faith and love for God and love for every person.

1.14.0.en: St. Paul declares the truth of God’s word, which gladdens a person who receives it and enjoys it, and this word is that Christ became incarnate to save sinners, that is, all humanity; and in humility and repentance he declares himself the chief of sinners because of his persecution of the Christians mentioned before.

1.15.0.en: Paul shows God’s wisdom and love in accepting him despite his sins and turning him into a minister, for this shows God’s longsuffering toward sinners, so as to encourage all the wicked to return to God, not only that He may forgive them but that He may give them the Kingdom of Heaven.

1.16.0.en: The Apostle ends his discourse on God’s mercy by glorifying Him, declaring some of His attributes: that He is eternal, that He is King in every age, that He is too high for anyone to see, and that in Him is all wisdom and honor.

1.16.1.en: What happened with Paul encourages us all to repent, however great or repeated our sins may be, and it urges us to a positive life with God through good works and serving others.

1.17.0.en: This commandment: Christ is the Savior of sinners, so we rely on Him.

1.17.1.en: The prophecies: there were earlier prophecies about Timothy, that he would live with God and be His minister. War a good warfare: strive in relying on God and in encouraging all sinners to repent so that they may obtain eternal life.

1.17.2.en: If God chose Timothy and declared that in prophecies about him, then Paul charges him to care for the salvation of his own soul and to call sinners to repentance.

1.18.0.en: Faith: reliance on the power of Christ working in him.

1.18.1.en: A good conscience: purity and sincerity in loving God and serving Him.

1.18.2.en: Having put away: some, that is, the heretics.

1.18.3.en: Have made shipwreck concerning faith: they went astray and sank, that is, they departed from Christ, and their hope and faith were lost.

1.18.4.en: The Apostle calls him to hold fast to the faith and purity of heart which the heretics rejected, and so went on the way of perdition.

1.19.0.en: Hymenaeus: he is also mentioned in (2 Tim 2:17), where Paul describes him as having erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection is past already, and so overthrowing the faith of some.

1.19.1.en: Alexander: he is the one mentioned in (2 Tim 4:14), “Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works.”

1.19.2.en: The pride of their hearts led these two persons to invent unsound teachings; therefore St. Paul decided to judge them by cutting them off from the fellowship of the Church, so that they would not corrupt the thoughts of the believers, and at the same time, by being deprived of fellowship, they might return to God in repentance. For the Apostle does not seek vengeance by the punishment, but asks for discipline that leads to correction.

2.0.0.en: After showing God’s mercy to all sinners, St. Paul declares the first of his teachings to Timothy in his shepherding of the Church, which is that he should call the believers to feel for all people, so that they offer up to Him their prayers for the needs of all and likewise give thanks to God for His gifts to all people.

2.0.1.en: It is fitting for us to care for everyone as our heavenly Father does, for this is the message of the Church, whether at the communal or the individual level; we do not ask only for what is for ourselves, but also for what is for others. And as the Church practices these kinds of prayers in her liturgical prayers, as in the Divine Liturgy, may you too, in your prayer, take care to ask for others, especially those who asked you to pray for them and those who have no one to remember them, that is, the despised and the rejected.

2.1.0.en: The Church is not an institution that competes with the world for what belongs to it, but a community that worships God for the sanctification of the world. So she offers supplications, prayers and intercessions for kings and rulers and those in positions of leadership, that God’s peace may come upon the land and that this may help the believers grow in godliness and the fear of God.

2.1.1.en: And these prayers for others gladden God’s heart and make our prayers acceptable and good before Him. We find in the Liturgy of St. Basil, before the prayer of reconciliation, the litany for the peace of the Church, and in the Liturgy of St. Gregory a litany for the king or president or those who serve in the court (the palace), and for all who work in the state and the soldiers, for their peace.

2.2.0.en: God rejoices in our prayers for everyone because He desires the salvation of all and calls them to know Him, for He is the true God, and so He rescues them from the error of idols and the sins of the world.

2.3.0.en: Here the Apostle sets forth a truth of faith, which is that there is one Mediator between God and men, and He is the incarnate Christ. He set this forth to refute what the Gnostics claimed of successive emanations from God, which they called “aeons,” that bring knowledge to people as the way of salvation. In their view Christ is the first step, that is, the first aeon, who raises man by knowledge to a greater aeon, and so on, until he reaches perfect knowledge, the Supreme Being.

2.3.1.en: So the Apostle replies to this and says that Christ is the only Mediator of atonement, and not the many mediating gods proclaimed by the Gnostics. And this, of course, has no relation to the intercession of the saints before God, because some use this verse to oppose our belief in the intercession of the saints; but it has nothing to do with intercession, rather it is a reply to the Gnostics.

2.4.0.en: The testimony: Christ’s redemption of humanity and the offering of His blood as atonement and justification for everyone who believes in Him. In due time: the time appointed by God for the redemption of man, that is, the time in which Christ died and rose.

2.4.1.en: Christ gave His life on the Cross, and by this He testified before the Father to the possibility of justifying man, so that everyone who believes in Him may enter into eternal life.

2.5.0.en: This is the salvation that St. Paul preaches, proclaiming the true faith to the Gentiles who were formerly idolaters, as God’s grace extended to embrace all humanity and the knowledge of the truth was no longer confined to one nation to the exclusion of another.

2.5.1.en: Christ bore witness to your righteousness before God by His death on the Cross; so you too must bear witness by your purity and your love for everyone, that Christ may be glorified in your good works.

2.6.0.en: Every where: Jewish worship was only in the temple at Jerusalem, but the churches of the New Testament are everywhere, in addition to private prayers in the inner room.

2.6.1.en: Holy hands: he means purity of body and spirit, so that men do not allow themselves uncleanness, for their prayers would not be accepted.

2.6.2.en: Without wrath: men are quick to anger, so he warns them to control themselves and keep their inner peace so that they may be able to pray and to sense God.

2.6.3.en: Doubting: men tend to rely on reason, and this may cast them into a troublesome debate that robs them of their peace, so he warns them against this so that they may concentrate in their prayers.

2.6.4.en: The Apostle calls the believing men to pray in their churches and their homes, joining their prayers with pure conduct, keeping away from anger and pride and the useless debate that results from them.

2.7.0.en: Modest apparel: clothing that is not a stumbling block.

2.7.1.en: Godliness: piety and the fear of God, that is, their conduct is fitting for daughters of God.

2.7.2.en: Sobriety: composure and not being preoccupied with appearance.

2.7.3.en: Broided hair: some women used to make dozens of braids in their hair, which consumed much time and attention, so the Apostle forbids excessive concern for adornment.

2.7.4.en: Gold or pearls: he means being preoccupied with adorning oneself abundantly with jewels.

2.7.5.en: He calls the believing women to commit to modest clothing that is not a stumbling block, as women who fear God, and not to be absorbed in adornment, whether in hair or ornaments or clothes.

2.8.0.en: Here he adds the positive side, for she who professes to live to God will surely care about her good works, and not only about keeping away from causing others to stumble.

2.9.0.en: The Apostle asks the woman not to speak in the church, but to hear the words of preaching from the man and to submit to his leadership, for this suits her and gives her rest as a woman; and he certainly does not mean to despise her or belittle her, because she can surpass the man in her holiness according to her faith and her life with God.

2.10.0.en: The Apostle forbids women to teach men, because leadership and teaching suit the man, and the woman is a help meet for him who completes him and supports him. The nature of the man does not accept teaching and leadership from the woman, whereas it suits the woman to be led and taught by the man. But the woman’s abstaining from teaching the man does not hinder her from teaching women, girls and children.

2.11.0.en: The idea of the woman’s submission to the man is not born of human thought, but is a divine order realized in creation, for God created Adam first and after him created the woman as a helper for him.

2.12.0.en: The serpent deceived Eve, and she broke the commandment, but Adam was not deceived, though he fell under Eve’s influence, for she is more exposed to deception. In this verse St. Paul shows us why a woman ought not to take up teaching: because she is affected more quickly than the man by her emotions, and so she may deviate from sound teaching, and it does not suit her to lead the teaching. But she can be more spiritual than the man through her emotions if she uses them well.

2.13.0.en: Just as the man has the responsibility of leadership and teaching, which qualifies him to obtain the heavenly crowns, so the woman has her responsibilities, such as raising her sons and daughters in virtue and helping them grow spiritually, so that she presents to the Church blessed members; and by this she has a share in the crowns of glory, on condition that she continue in faith and love and holiness with wisdom, which is the true adornment of a woman.

2.13.1.en: Do not be distracted from the love of Christ by any earthly matter, and so you will be able to open yourself in prayer with a pure heart and enjoy the divine sense; and what helps you in this is to put the fear of God before your eyes, so that you reject every sin and keep your purity.

2.13.2.en: The Church and the requirements for the priestly ranks
